newsitem.title: USA: Overhaul planned for US forest laws - Senate aide.
newsitem.headline: Overhaul planned for US forest laws - Senate aide.

text.p: Leaders of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee plan to propose a comprehensive overhaul of U.S. forestry laws, a key aide said Tuesday.
The aide, Mark Rey, said details would be provided in early December.
In general, he said, the bill would increase forest management options and give weight to on-the-ground expertise. It would be "comprehensive" and contain seven sections.

Agriculture Undersecretary Jim Lyons, who appeared at a think-tank symposium with Rey, said the Clinton administration was drafting its own proposals to modernize forest planning. He said it would be "more fine-tuning than radical surgery."

Lyons said the administration's priorities included "addressing legitimate forest health issues," more efficient operation of the Forest Service and improving the mix of "products"," such as timber and recreation, in the 191 million acres of national forests and grasslands.

"Cutting the public out of discussions is not part of the equation," Lyons said in remarks apparently aimed at the so-called "salvage rider" approved by Congress It ordered an increase in timber sales and limited the right to object.
Rey said the new bill, rather than restricting appeals, might broaden the right to sue over forest regulations.
It also might try to "develop processes for community-based solutions" to local forest issues. Rey also said rather than setting "timber targets," the bill would focus on "resource outcomes."

Brock Evans, president of the Federation of Western Outdoors Clubs and another speaker at the symposium, said timber industry groups and allies in Congress wanted to amend forest laws so they could cut more timber. Talk about forest management or giving discretion to forest operators was a smokescreen, he said, for "get on with the logging."
Evans forecast "a stalemate again" on logging policy.

Timber harvest on federal land has dropped to about four billion board feet a year, compared to more than 10 billion a year in the late 1980s. The decline was due to court rulings and steps to protect rare animals and plants, particularly in the Pacific Northwest.
Rey said the new bill would not be a replate of legislation offered in the past two years.

Doug Crandall, an official of the American Forest and Paper Association, a trade group, advocated a strong local role in forestry operations. "Somehow, we've got to structure the process so the input is there," he said.
